thread.title: AIEQ - Should Invest In An AI Portfolio? - AI Powered Equity ETF (NYSEARCA:AIEQ)

author: Kurtis Hemmerling
title: AIEQ - Should Invest In An AI Portfolio? - AI Powered Equity ETF (NYSEARCA:AIEQ)
text:
Should you invest in AI-powered portfolios? The short answer is this: yes, no and maybe . Why do I have three answers for a single question? Because I am addressing three different types of investors.
An AI powered portfolio makes sense if you already have a portion of your portfolio with a discretionary manager, which is essentially what you get with AIEQ ( AIEQ ). If you are a DIY investor who needs to understand the underlying strategy and requires a narrative of portfolio performance, this is likely the wrong product for you. It might be useful to use a partial AI portfolio where some of the tasks are delegated while the overall strategy is determined by you. Before we consider each of these 3 scenarios, let's have a quick peek under the hood at one description of how the AI which powers AIEQ works. If you already know a little on the topic or you don't care, skip down to the heading Who Should Buy AIEQ.
The T-800 Is Not Your AI Financial Advisor
A Blurb About How IBM Watson Works The following is an incredibly brief summary of the video about IBM Watson , which is the AI powering the AIEQ ETF. When you watch the video, you will notice the use of the term 'cognitive computing' which refers to a high level type of learning which is more similar to how humans operate and less like traditional programming.
Here is a quick overview of some of the steps:
A corpus of knowledge, or financial literacy in our example, is curated by a human. High quality relevant materials are fed into Watson’s brain. This information is ingested and organized. A human expert trains Watson on how to interpret the information with machine learning algorithms. Question and answer pairs are fed to Watson. Watson continues to learn through ongoing interaction with data points such as financial tweets, articles, SEC filings and more. A human will periodically review Watson's process to ensure calibration. Watson will analyze data to uncover insights and form hypotheses, look for evidence to support it, and create a weighted score of its confidence in such predictions. While cognitive computing has human interaction at many different points in the process, it is not 100% transparent. The AI may be unable to explain exactly why it made a certain decision any more than a human can. It may come up with a narrative which may or may not be completely accurate.
Who Should Buy AIEQ Do you already employ a discretionary investment manager for a portion of your portfolio? If so, then an AI-powered fund such as AIEQ might add some interesting diversification in that capital allocation.
A discretionary manager has authority to make certain buy and sell decisions for a client. If you are already comfortable with allowing another entity to make such decisions for you, you may be a good candidate for allowing an AI to recommend investments based on its unique insights. You are probably someone who does not need a narrative on every trade that your discretionary manager makes. He has targeted knowledge coupled with intuition and you are willing to take a punt with him.
The same could be said of AIEQ. Will the actual insights of the AI be more valuable than a human? That is what you must be willing to find out. But don’t expect to understand or be given a story as to why it does what it does. And when the trades turn out poorly, you are likely to only hear ‘well, it learns from its mistakes so it should be smarter now’ as your explanation as to why you should stay invested. If you are comfortable with that – then AIEQ might be right for you.
Who Should Maybe Avoid AIEQ? AIEQ is not for everyone. Are you the type of investor who trades in a very specific manner? Perhaps you only trade gold stocks or a certain sub-set of value stocks. Maybe you only buy high yielding blue-chips or micro-cap momentum stocks. If so, you would likely struggle with an ETF such as AIEQ which is not fettered to any specific strategy. Look at the diversity of holdings.
AIEQ holds mega-caps such as Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ), Amazon ( AMZN ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ) while also holding micro- and small-cap stocks such as LSB Industries ( LXU ) and Intra-Cellular Therapies ( ITCI ). It buys high-yielders such as BGC Partners ( BGCP ) and Ares Capital Corp ( ARCC ) while also holding over 40 stocks which do not have dividends. Many stocks have a P/E ratio of less than 10 while others have a P/E ratio of more than 1,000. If you require a very specific stock universe or strategy, then AIEQ is probably not for you. But more than that, if you do not have confidence in the overall process, if you begin to second guess the value of an AI portfolio at any point, the results could be disastrous. How so?
Who Should Definitely Avoid AIEQ? Do you require a narrative as to why a strategy or stock is behaving in a certain way?
Imagine you hold a stock which you believe to be a good long-term bet. Then the stock goes down 10%. And then another 10%. And yet another 10%. The market is up 20% and you are down 30%. What are you going to do? If you feel that you have a reasonable explanation as to why your stock is under-performing, you might hold through such under-performance as you wait for other investors to realize this potential hidden gem. But what if the stock was dropping like a rock without any discernible reason? Worse yet, what if your entire stock trading strategy, such as value momentum, was losing while the entire market was winning? How long before you cut your losses and switched styles?
Market Is Up - Strategy Is Down
This is one very real possibility when investing in a product which has no narrative. If the AI under-performs the market by 30%, would you feel comfortable holding without knowing why? Is the AI making bad insights or are the opportunities being undervalued and future out-performance is in store? There is no way to know for certain. You might decide to abandon ship at precisely the wrong time much like when an investor pulls out at the bottom of a bear market just before the greatest rally of all time. Or you might save what little is left of that allocation. That is a big unknown when it comes to investing in a somewhat 'black box' process...at least for us.
If the above describes you, then AIEQ is likely the wrong investment.
The Hybrid Approach With AI But there is another option that might work for you. Perhaps you believe that the AI could have some utility in your investment process but you are uncomfortable handing over full control to a machine. In such a circumstance, you should consider employing the services of a firm which can integrate with your existing investment process. This is probably a more feasible option for an investment house or hedge fund looking for additional edge rather than a single retail investor due to the cost of employing such a service.
Since I am trialing the services of Kavout , I will use them as an example of how this process might work.
Kavout uses machine learning and deep learning processes to develop what they call a 'K Score'. K Scores are created by their AI called Kai (as opposed to IBM Watson). Kai combines various fundamental and technical factors along with alternative data which has historically resulted in out-performance. The stock scores range from 1 to 9.
AI Can Concentrate a Large Portfolio Suppose you have an existing strategy where you buy deep value momentum stocks with positive earnings revisions. Or some other small-cap strategy which has strong academic backing and you feel comfortable trading it even during periods of prolonged draw-down. You might have a screened list of the top 300 stocks according to this strategy, but you are looking for a way to select just 50.
An Actual 300 Stock Smallcap System (Simulated Performance Jan 1999 – Dec 2018)
You could painstakingly have a team go through this list by hand every day or week or you could delegate this task utilizing your AI service. This is just one way in which I feel that AI could augment human decision makers while still sticking to an over-arching strategy that you feel confident in.
Charting Signals Using AI Another way to use an AI service is with chart pattern and price forecasts. Perhaps you already have a basket of stocks to buy. Your typical procedure is to just use a trading algo and buy Monday morning. But what if an AI service could analyze chart patterns and give you recommendations with probabilities and time horizons? Maybe the best time to buy the stock is in a week or two. Maybe one of the stocks on your list is forming a bearish pattern. Possibly one stock is making all the right moves and you should double-down. This is another hybrid approach that I see as a real possibility that doesn’t hand over full control to an AI.
AI Screened Cup and Handle Patterns
Some Difficult Questions But some difficult questions are raised as regards to AI that I cannot answer satisfactorily. One question is how do you differentiate between the various AI platforms?
For instance, I compared the holdings of the AIEQ ETF with Kavout’s Kai Score.
Both agreed that Costco ( COST ) and Splunk ( SPLK ) where highly desirable stocks. Other holdings of AIEQ were ranked near the very bottom of K Score such as Netflix ( NFLX ), Valero Energy ( VLO ) and Amazon ( AMZN ). Who is right and who is wrong if you cannot understand the inner workings of the system? Or perhaps they are both correct but targeting different holding periods? A short-term sell but a long-term buy? Or the other way around?
Exactly how do you compare and shop for the right AI that would suit your style and methodology? Do you base it on the quality and type of the data being fed in? The team that designed the AI? Perhaps the various artificial intelligence's can be pitted against each other in some sort of powerlifting contest which will have meaningful insights into their comparative abilities. As well, if the underlying scoring system is constantly evolving, how meaningful is past performance?
I don’t have the answers but I do find the topic interesting and worthy of further discussion. My own knowledge on the topic is limited and perhaps some AI expert needs to educate us laymen so that we can have more confidence in a process that is not well understood by most.
In the end, AIEQ is an interesting fund blazing some new ground that might be suitable for an investor willing to let a computer be their discretionary manager for a portion of their fund.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
